title: WITAWITADD - Exploration!
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Sf25ENrbQGM

The big one. Daniel (@dungeondive) argues that no board game actually contains exploration — the components are finite, the box has a bottom — so what matters is which games best sustain the *illusion* of it. He breaks that illusion into five parts.

First, the sense that anything can happen, achieved either through sheer volume (Shadows of Brimstone, whose encounter decks he reshuffles wholesale so something new always feels just out of reach) or through Secrets of the Lost Tomb's stacks of misadventures. Second, mystery: Warhammer Quest Silver Tower, which he'll happily call the better-designed game than the 1995 original; Tales of the Arabian Nights; and City of Chaos, whose puzzle he says he is still thinking about. Third, unpredictable map layouts — tiles laid as you go, Advanced HeroQuest perhaps the purest example. Fourth, a balance of combat and non-combat encounters, which is where he defends the uneventful stretch as authentically adventurer-ish. Fifth, genuine discovery, where knowledge accrues to the *player*: The 7th Continent's remembered map, and Forgotten Depths.

Forgotten Depths is the video's revelation, and the reason he made the episode. Its legendary locations are marked by tetromino-like tile shapes, so the player must lay the map deliberately to make that shape appear before the characters can reach the site. A fourth-wall-breaking tile-laying mini-game inside a crawl — and he admits he wishes he'd thought of it for his own design.

----

Which of the five — anything-can-happen, mystery, random maps, encounter balance, or real discovery — matters most to you? And which game nails your favourite?
